items.title: Crystal Explained: Ruby's Syntax, Compiled Speed
items.author: The Practical Developer
items.content:
Ruby is beloved for its readable syntax and developer happiness, and criticised for its speed. Crystal, released in 2014, asks a simple question: what if you kept Ruby's syntax and compiled it to native code? The result is a statically typed, compiled language that reads almost like Ruby, runs close to C speed, and needs no virtual machine. It is still young, but it is the most elegant answer yet to the dynamic-versus-compiled trade-off.

Ruby-like syntax, static types, and native compilation

Crystal's model rests on a few distinctive ideas:

  • : blocks, symbols, and expressive method calls, so Ruby developers feel at home immediately.
  • Static typing with inference: types are checked at compile time, but usually inferred, so you get safety without annotating everything.
  • : code that writes code at compile time, replacing Ruby's metaprogramming with a safer, checked version of the same power.
  • : Crystal compiles to a single binary via LLVM, with no runtime to install, so deployment is a file, not a stack.

A tiny example shows the shape: it reads like Ruby, but the compiler checks it:

is a typed instance variable; is string interpolation, exactly as in Ruby. Same joy, checked by a compiler, running natively.

Crystal's trade is youth: a small ecosystem, fewer libraries and jobs than Ruby or Go, and tooling that is still maturing. Windows support has historically lagged, and the community is small. Choose Crystal when you love Ruby's syntax but need compiled speed and single-binary deployment, choose Go when ecosystem and hiring dominate, and choose Ruby when the existing ecosystem matters most.

Compiled speed, Ruby syntax

Crystal is Ruby's syntax at compiled speed: inferred static types, macros, and native binaries, in code that reads like Ruby. It trades ecosystem maturity for elegance and performance, and for Rubyists who want speed without leaving home, that trade is tempting.

items.title: Object Allocation and Reuse in Crystal Iterators
items.author: kojix2
items.content:
When writing C bindings in Crystal, one question often arises.

Should an object yielded by be newly created on every iteration, or should the same object be reused?

My understanding of this issue is still incomplete, but I would like to summarize my current thoughts.

First, why use Crystal rather than Ruby to write C bindings?

The main reason is performance.

Memory allocation is an important consideration when writing high-performance Crystal code. Crystal uses garbage collection, and memory allocation and garbage collection have associated costs. It is also difficult to control exactly when memory is reclaimed.

These costs are usually not a major concern, but they can become important when writing C bindings.

Consider iterating over a collection:

To execute this code efficiently, should a new object be allocated on every iteration?

If a new object is created each time, and the object refers to memory managed by C, should the underlying data also be copied?

One important consideration is compatibility with .

To use safely, objects yielded by must remain valid when they are stored for later use.

For example, and collect elements into an array. If the same object is reused on every iteration, the array will contain multiple references to that object.

Therefore, when performance is not critical, creating independent objects is a reasonable choice.

However, when performance is important, the situation is different. Benchmarks show that memory allocation, copying, and garbage collection can significantly reduce performance.

In Ruby, safety would generally take priority. In Crystal, however, performance closer to C is often an important goal. It is therefore desirable to avoid unnecessary memory allocation and garbage collection.

A similar design can be found in Crystal's standard library: .

By default, creates a new array on each iteration. When is specified, the same array is reused.

This allows the programmer to explicitly choose object reuse when performance is important.

However, using an argument to switch between different behaviors within the same method may complicate implementation, type inference, and optimization.

Another approach is to provide separate methods. Possible names include:

    There does not yet appear to be an established naming convention for this distinction in the Crystal community.

    Another possible design is to make reuse objects by default and implement the necessary -like methods separately. This approach gives priority to performance.

    It is important to distinguish between reusing a Crystal object and borrowing memory from C. These are different concepts. Whether or is the appropriate name depends on how memory ownership is managed.

    Other related questions remain. For example, should implement ? Who should own the memory allocated by C, and when should that memory be released?

    (This post was translated from the original Japanese post using ChatGPT)

items.title: How to Improve Your Coding Skills: Practical Tips for Developers
items.author: zift
items.content:
Learning to code is not just about understanding programming syntax. It is about developing problem-solving skills, writing efficient solutions, and learning how to build applications that work in real-world situations. Whether you are a beginner or an experienced developer, consistent practice and the right learning approach can help you become a better programmer.

1. Build a Strong Programming Foundation

Start by understanding variables, data types, loops, conditional statements, functions, and object-oriented programming. These concepts form the foundation of almost every programming language. Instead of memorizing syntax, focus on understanding how and why each concept works.

2. Practice Data Structures and Algorithms

Data structures and algorithms help developers solve problems efficiently. Begin with arrays, strings, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and hash maps. Once you understand the basics, practice searching, sorting, recursion, and dynamic programming.

Try solving problems independently before looking at solutions. Platforms such as TheZift can help developers practice coding problems, strengthen their logical thinking, and prepare for technical interviews.

Practical projects turn theoretical knowledge into useful skills. Start with small applications such as a task manager, calculator, weather dashboard, or personal portfolio. Gradually move toward projects involving APIs, databases, authentication, and deployment.

Building projects also teaches you how to debug errors, organize code, and understand the complete software development process.

4. Learn to Debug Effectively

Debugging is an essential part of software development. When something goes wrong, read the error message carefully, reproduce the issue, and isolate the problematic section of code. Use debugging tools and logs instead of changing multiple things randomly.

Learning to identify the root cause of a problem will make you more independent and confident as a developer.

5. Maintain a Consistent Learning Routine

Consistency matters more than occasional long study sessions. Spend time each day solving problems, reviewing concepts, reading documentation, or improving an existing project. Keep track of what you learn and revisit topics that you find difficult.

You can also explore tutorials, coding challenges, and developer communities to discover different approaches to solving technical problems.

Improving your coding skills requires patience, regular practice, and a willingness to learn from mistakes. Focus on strong fundamentals, solve problems consistently, build practical projects, and develop effective debugging habits. Over time, these small efforts can help you become a more capable developer and prepare you for new technical challenges.

items.title: Python 3.10 just went end-of-life, and my stdlib-only tool doesn't care
items.author: Damiano
items.content:
Yesterday the Python team shipped 3.15.1 and 3.14.9. The release I actually care about this month is a different one: on October 1, 2026, Python 3.10 reached end of life. No more bugfix releases, no more security patches. 3.10.22 is the last one, forever.

I know this because a small tool of mine runs on it.

I built a small offline utility for myself that reads Swiss administrative letters - payment orders, reminders, official forms - and extracts the parts that matter: who wants money, how much, by when. It runs locally, with the model on localhost, which is the whole point: these letters contain exactly the data you don't paste into a chatbot.

The constraint I gave myself was brutal and deliberate: Python standard library only. No pip install, no packages, no virtualenv. The result is about 306 lines of plain Python that can run with whatever interpreter is already there.

That interpreter, on that machine, is Python 3.10.

Why I pinned myself to 3.10 in the first place

Choosing "stdlib only" sounds like a purist stance. It was actually an operational one. Every dependency is a supply chain you have to watch. Every install is a small ceremony. The standard library, on the other hand, is just there - same version as the interpreter, tested together, no network required.

The side effect I didn't fully think through: pinning to stdlib quietly pins you to the interpreter too. My code uses nothing newer than 3.10, so it runs everywhere from 3.10 up. But the machine itself still carries 3.10, and as of this month, that version gets nothing. Not even security fixes.

What end-of-life actually means here

Let me be precise, because "EOL" gets thrown around loosely. Python 3.10 entered security-only mode back in 2023, which means it has only received security patches since then. As of October 1, 2026, it receives nothing at all. If a vulnerability is found in the 3.10 interpreter tomorrow, there will be no official fix.

How much does that matter for my tool? Less than for a web service, more than zero. My threat model is narrow but real: the program handles letter text that arrives from outside. A maliciously crafted document attacking an unpatched interpreter bug is a theoretical attack path. For an offline single-user tool, it's a path I'm willing to walk for a few more weeks, not a path I want to live on.

The upgrade is cheap, and that's the payoff

Here's the part that makes me glad about the stdlib decision. Migrating a project off an EOL Python is usually painful because of dependencies: some package pins an old version, some C extension needs rebuilding, some transitive thing breaks. I have none of that. My entire dependency tree is the standard library, and the standard library's promise is backwards compatibility within reason.

So the plan is boring: install 3.15, run the tool, run a handful of test letters through it, compare outputs. If 306 lines of stdlib Python don't survive a five-version jump, something has gone very wrong in the world. The release notes for 3.15 even work in my favor: UTF-8 is now the default encoding (PEP 686), which removes one of the few places where my file-reading code could behave differently across systems.

There's also one new 3.15 feature that fits the tool's shape: explicit lazy imports (PEP 810). The tool starts, reads one letter, prints, exits. Startup time is most of its runtime. Lazy imports are made for exactly this shape of program.

Dependencies are a bet. Every package you add is a bet that someone will keep maintaining it, that it will keep working with your Python version, and that you'll be online when you need to fix it. For this tool I bet on the standard library, and the bet paid off in an unexpected place: end-of-life day. When your Python version dies, the size of your problem is roughly the size of your dependency tree. Mine is zero packages, so my problem is an afternoon, not a project.

If you maintain anything still on 3.10 - and a lot of long-lived internal tools are - the clock that started on October 1 is real. The good news from yesterday's releases is that the landing spot is excellent. 3.15.1 is waiting.

items.title: Hotwire Marten: Updating Just the Parts That Changed
items.author: Marvin Ahlgrimm
items.content:
In the first part, we wired up Hotwire in a Marten application and built a small task list. Clicking "Create task" loaded a form into a Turbo Frame. Pretty nice for something that barely involved JavaScript!

But a task app where you can't complete a task feels a little broken. Nothing is done or is everything already done? Or maybe I just forgot to add some mechanisms for that 🤷🏻.

Let's fix that with Turbo Streams. New tasks should appear in the list without a full page reload, completing a task should update just that item, and deleting one should remove it.

Turbo, Stimulus, and importmap are already in place from the first part, so we can focus on the behavior this time. We'll start with task creation.

Before adding the streams, let's extract the markup for a task into src/templates/tasks/_task.html:

{{ task.title }}

The tag comes from marten-turbo. For a task with ID 42, it produces . We'll use that ID later to update or remove exactly this element.

In , replace the existing list with:

No tasks yet.
  {% for task in records %}
    {% include "tasks/_task.html" %}
  {% endfor %}

The surrounding "Create task" link and empty frame stay as they were. The list now has an ID too, so we can append things to it.

One small detail: the empty message is always in the HTML. A little CSS handles its visibility:

When a task appears, the message hides. When we delete the last task, it comes back. Conveniently, our stream responses don't have to do anything about it. Modern CSS is awesome!

Also add to . We're going to append new tasks at the bottom, so the initial page should use the same order. Otherwise a reload could rearrange our list. Small but important!

Creating a task with Turbo Streams

Our create handler already knows how to validate and save a task. We can keep that and switch its parent class to the Turbo-aware version:

tells the handler which template to render after a successful Turbo submission. makes the created record available as , matching the variable our partial already uses.

Now create src/templates/tasks/create.turbo_stream.html:

{% turbo_stream 'append' 'tasks' template: 'tasks/_task.html' %}
{% turbo_stream 'replace' 'new_task' do %}{% end_turbo_stream %}

That's the entire response template.

After saving, the task appears in the list and the form closes.

Why replace the frame instead of removing it? Our "Create task" link still needs that frame as its target. Replacing it also clears the attribute Turbo added when it loaded the form, so clicking the link again can fetch a fresh form.

A successful submission is the easy part. Let's submit an empty title.

We want the form to stay open and show the error from Marten. For that, move the frame and form into src/templates/tasks/_form.html:


    {% csrf_input %}
    Title:
    {% for error in schema.title.errors %}
      {{ error.message }}
    {% endfor %}
    Create

Then replace the frame in with {% include "tasks/_form.html" %}. Keep the page's template inheritance and content block around it.

I've removed the input's attribute here so we can actually send an empty title to Marten and see its validation response. The schema still validates the title on the server:

The old field is gone from this schema. Creating a task only needs a title; completion will get its own schema in a moment.

Add one more setting to :

And create that template:

{% turbo_stream 'replace' 'new_task' template: 'tasks/_form.html' %}

The handler returns a 422 response for invalid submissions and renders the form with Marten's validation errors. The form stays open so we can try again.

Finally, completing some work

Let's add a checkbox. First, a small schema in src/schemas/task_completion_schema.cr:

And an update handler in src/handlers/tasks/complete_handler.cr:

Add its route inside :

The handler only accepts POST requests. We don't need a separate page for editing one checkbox.

Its stream template, tasks/complete.turbo_stream.html, is another one-liner:

{% turbo_stream 'replace' task template: 'tasks/_task.html' %}

This time we pass the record itself as the target. The tag derives its DOM ID, so becomes something like , matching the from our partial.


    {% csrf_input %}
    Save{{ task.title }}

And give completed tasks a little styling:

Check the box and click Save. The task is saved and shown as completed.

There's a slightly sneaky detail in the form: the hidden input before the checkbox. An unchecked checkbox sends no value at all. We need an explicit to clear an existing completion value. When checked, both values are sent, and Marten takes the last one: .

If you've used Rails form helpers, this probably looks familiar.

A little Stimulus, finally

The Save button works, but clicking it after every checkbox change feels unnecessary. This is a good job for Stimulus.

marten stimulus generate controller autosubmit

Replace its generated contents with:

Then add the controller and action to the completion form:

The checkbox's event bubbles up to the form, where Stimulus calls . We can put the Save button inside so it's only displayed when JavaScript is disabled:

Save

Our importmap and controller loading were already configured in the first part. Rebuild and restart the server after adding the controller so its pin appears in the generated importmap.

Now clicking the checkbox submits the form, saves the task, and replaces the list item. Stimulus also connects the controller on the replacement form, so the next click works too.

And that's all the custom JavaScript for this feature. The controller doesn't even know what a task is. It just submits its form.

We can create and complete tasks now. Let's also add a way to delete them.

Create src/handlers/tasks/delete_handler.cr:

The handler also lets us return a directly from Crystal. For deletion, that saves us a template file.

And add a second form after the title's inside :


  {% csrf_input %}
  Delete

Click Delete, the record is deleted, and the stream removes its list item. If that was the last task, our empty message becomes visible again through CSS.

We now have a task list where creating, completing, and deleting tasks updates just the relevant elements on the page.

What I like about the Marten integration is how little we had to add to our existing handlers. We switched to the Turbo-aware base classes, configured the stream templates, and reused the same task partial throughout. The only custom JavaScript is our small autosubmit controller, but it feels SPA like nonetheless!

items.title: I Spent $184 on Chakra Crystals and Tracked Everything for 60 Days
items.author: Kui Luo
items.content:
Quick background so you know where I'm coming from: I'm a backend developer who builds small SaaS tools for a living. I trust logs more than feelings. If something claims to work, I want a before-and-after number. Six months ago, crystals were firmly in the same mental category as horoscopes for me — fun at parties, useless in production.

Then my sleep fell apart.

Not "I stayed up late coding" falling apart. I mean lying awake at 2 a.m. with my heart doing drum solos, checking my resting heart rate on a $30 fitness band and watching it sit at 78 bpm when my baseline had been 61. Three side projects, two clients, one very patient girlfriend, and exactly zero downtime. My doctor used the word "stress" four times in a single appointment.

Around that time my girlfriend left a black tourmaline stone on my nightstand. No lecture, just "try holding it when your brain won't shut up." I rolled my eyes, and then — because I'm incapable of trying anything casually — I turned it into a 60-day experiment with a spreadsheet. Here's the honest data, including the parts that made me uncomfortable.

The setup, so you can repeat it

I didn't want to rely on vibes, so:

  • No stones at all. Just tracking.
  • five 9-day blocks, each focused on one "chakra" area, using only that block's stones.
  • time to fall asleep (fitness band estimate plus my own note), resting heart rate, and a 3-line journal entry every night. Mood, anything weird, one line about work stress.
  • $200. I ended at $184.37.

I also did two things I'd recommend to anyone: I never changed my caffeine intake (2 coffees before noon, always), and I never decided on a "success number" in advance. I just wrote down what happened.

Block 1: grounding stones

Stones: hematite, black tourmaline. Cost: $23.

The pitch behind these is "grounding" — calming the racing-thoughts loop. I read the root chakra crystal guide on SagStone mostly to figure out which stones were even supposed to do what, and it's honestly more thorough than the Etsy listings I'd been squinting at.

Results: average time to fall asleep went from 41 minutes (baseline) to 28 minutes. Resting heart rate: 74 → 70. My journal from day 19 says "held the rock for like 5 min before bed, felt ridiculous, slept anyway."

Now, is that the rock or the ritual of lying down with no phone for five minutes? I genuinely can't tell you. Hold that thought.

Block 2: creativity stones

Stones: carnelian, orange calcite. Cost: $19.

This block was for the "I can't start writing this feature" problem. The sacral chakra stones guide frames these as creativity and emotional-flow stones.

Honest result: I procrastinated exactly the same way (an average of 47 minutes of "quick checks" before deep work, per RescueTime). The one difference: I journaled more freely that week — longer entries, more honest ones. Maybe the carnelian on my desk made journaling feel like less of a chore. Or maybe orange rocks are just nice to look at. I kept two of them on the desk anyway. Judge me.

Block 3: confidence stones before the biggest pitch of my year

Stones: citrine, tiger's eye. Cost: $31.

Timing was luck — day 37 landed two days before the most important client pitch I'd ever given. The solar plexus chakra guide describes these as confidence stones, and look: I'm not going to pretend a yellow rock closed a $9,000 contract. What I noticed is that I showed up calmer than usual. Pre-pitch resting heart rate: 82, versus 95+ before similar calls in the past.

My working theory: the stone gave my nervous system a specific physical thing to do with my hands and breath, instead of doom-refreshing my inbox. That's worth $31 even if it's pure placebo with good marketing.

Block 4: the one that actually surprised me

Stones: rose quartz, green aventurine. Cost: $27.

This is the block I expected to be pure nonsense — heart chakra stones for, quote, "love and emotional healing." I mostly did it for completeness.

But my journal that week has three separate entries about arguments with my girlfriend that de-escalated instead of escalating. Count of actual fights in the 9-day block: 1. The 9 days before: 4. And no, the pitch win doesn't explain it — the win came a week earlier, and historically good weeks make us fight MORE, because I get insufferable.

My best non-magical explanation: I already had a nightly wind-down ritual by then, and she joined it sometimes. Ten quiet minutes in the same room does more for a relationship than any stone. But the rose quartz is what got us into the room. Fine. Point taken, universe.

Block 5: sleep, round two

Stones: amethyst, lepidolite. Cost: $34.

Amethyst is THE sleep crystal according to every list on the internet. By this point my sleep was already much better (22-minute average to fall asleep), so this block was a "can it hold the gains" test.

It held. 24-minute average, no breakthrough, no regression. My band's sleep score for the final week: 84, up from a baseline of 63.

The uncomfortable conclusion

If you came here for "crystals are fake" or "crystals changed my life," you'll be disappointed: the rocks are probably placebo, and the placebo still outperformed my previous coping mechanism, which was scrolling Hacker News at 1 a.m.

What I think actually happened: crystal healing works as a ritual scaffold. The stone is a physical prompt that says "the day is over now." Five minutes of sitting still with a rock beats five minutes of a phone screen, and it compounds. Would plain meditation with no rock have worked as well or better? Probably. But I never managed to build a meditation habit in 4 years of trying, and I built this habit in 60 days because the rock gave it a handle.

Skeptics: we won. The mystical claims are unfalsifiable and I'm not defending them. But if a $184 pile of rocks is the entry fee to a working wind-down routine for an overworked developer, I've paid more for worse software.

If you want to try this without getting scammed

Hard-won advice, take it or leave it:

  1. Cap your spend at $50 for a first kit. Everything I used cost under $40 per block, and the cheap stones worked as "well" as the pretty ones. The beginner's crystal healing guide on SagStone has a sane starter list — that's where I'd point a friend, instead of some $90 "supercharged bundle."
  2. Buy from shops with real, individual photos. Dyed glass sold as amethyst is everywhere. If a shop can't tell you the stone's origin region, skip it.
  3. Mine was time-to-sleep. If you can't name your metric, you're buying decoration, not running an experiment.
  4. Skip anything over $50 with healing claims attached. It's the same rock.
  5. "Cleansing" costs nothing. Water, moonlight, done. Anyone selling you a $25 cleansing kit is selling you moonlight.

Six months later, here's what's still true: I sleep around 7 hours, my resting heart rate is back to 63, and there are eleven rocks on my desk that my coworkers absolutely roast me for. I can't prove the rocks did anything mystical. I can prove that on day 1 I couldn't fall asleep before 1 a.m., and today I can't stay awake past 11.

Whatever that's worth to you, it was worth $184.37 to me.

items.title: A language for humans and computers: Crystal in the AI era
items.author: Marvin Ahlgrimm
items.content:
At Rails World 2026, DHH described a division of labour that caught my attention: let agents write Rust and enjoy the result without having to look at the code.

I can see the appeal, and I see the same sentiment at my workplace. When an agent writes the code, the effort of writing it by hand matters less. The compiler can catch mistakes as the agent works.

But I still need and want to understand the software I am responsible for. For me, that points to Crystal.

Familiar syntax, static checks

That familiarity matters even when I am no longer typing every line. I still read the implementation, question its choices and make changes myself. Type inference keeps many annotations out of the way while the compiler checks how values are used.

Static checks on nullable values are available in other languages, too. What interests me about Crystal is having those checks in code I find straightforward to read. The agent gets feedback from the compiler; I get an implementation I can work with.

A compiler cannot choose the right tools

How do I know the agent chose the right libraries and integration approach?

Later in the talk, around 32:15, DHH describes assigning work asynchronously and reviewing the result. In my projects, that review includes the choices inside the implementation.

I recently tried setting up a small Marten application with only one prompt. During implementation, I had to correct the agent twice:

  • I wanted Marten Turbo and Marten Stimulus. The agent used npm to install the JavaScript packages instead of the CLI provided by Marten-importmap, which was the integration approach I wanted.
  • It started developing its own throttling middleware instead of using Marten-throttle.

I maintain these Marten shards, so I recognised the detours. npm was not the setup I wanted, and the custom middleware would have given me more code to maintain. Neither choice was a type error. Correcting them took knowledge of the project and its libraries.

Where compiler feedback has helped me

A few months ago, when the models I used were less capable, I repeatedly saw compilation errors in generated Crystal code. Some involved incorrect handling of values. In some cases, compiler feedback led the agent towards a correction without me having to explain the type problem myself.

A small example shows what the compiler can catch:

The first argument might be missing. Its type is , also written . Calling directly is rejected because does not provide that method.

An ordinary conditional handles the missing value:

Inside the branch, the compiler knows the local variable cannot be . Crystal documents this type narrowing and its limitations, including why repeated getter calls cannot always be narrowed in the same way.

Writing another / can feel tedious. I appreciate it more when an agent writes the code: I can see what it decided to do when the argument is missing.

Compiling still leaves a decision open

There is another way to get past the error:

This compiles, but raises an exception when the argument is missing. The standard-library documentation describes that behaviour and recommends avoiding where possible.

Ameba's rule flags the assertion in this example. With the rule enabled, the linter gives the agent feedback about a shortcut the compiler accepts.

The requirement is still open. Should a missing name produce a guest label? Should it stop the operation? Is absence supposed to be impossible? The compiler accepts both the guest fallback and the assertion. I still have to decide which matches the requirement.

I still need end-to-end checks in both Marten applications and fixes or features for Meridian, my deployment tool. Parts of that work can already be automated, but the agents I use do not reliably cover all my requirements.

Code and tests generated from the same misunderstanding can agree with each other.

Libraries and compiler feedback

The Marten experiment showed that I cannot assume the agent will find the libraries I want. In a smaller ecosystem, I need to name them and provide current documentation.

Waiting for the compiler also adds up. Long development builds slow down every round of corrections.

The Generative Compilation preprint explores compiler feedback during the generation of partial Rust programs and reports improvements over feedback after complete generation. Its results suggest that the timing of compiler feedback matters as well as the checks themselves.

I have not benchmarked my Crystal workflow against Rust. If you work with Rust every day, you may find its code easier to review.

Crystal can be hard to read, too. Complex macros can hide what the code does, and its unsafe operations need careful review. I have to account for that effort even when an agent handles the implementation.

The code I still want to understand

I expect agents to do more implementation work. In my projects, I still need and want to judge the result, check requirements and understand enough to make changes.

With Crystal, static feedback helps the agent correct certain mistakes, and its syntax helps me inspect the decisions that remain.

Crystal calls itself a language for humans and computers. As computers take on more of the writing, the human side becomes a reason to choose it. I want to delegate implementation and remain capable of understanding and changing the result. Crystal makes that practical for me.
